lessons.title: Chord inversions: a, b and c

objectives: A triad can be arranged with any of its three notes in the bass — this is its position, or inversion
Root position (a) has the root in the bass; 1st inversion (b) has the 3rd in the bass; 2nd inversion (c) has the 5th in the bass
Name a chord in two steps: work out the triad (I, II, IV or V) by finding its root, then read the bass note to name the position — so a IV chord with its 3rd in the bass is IVb

concept.title: Chord inversions: a, b and c
concept.body: The same triad can be built up from any of its three notes. When the root is the lowest note the chord is in ROOT POSITION (a). When the 3rd is the lowest note it is in 1ST INVERSION (b). When the 5th is the lowest note it is in 2ND INVERSION (c). The notes are the same — only which one sits at the bottom changes. To name an inverted chord, first find the root by stacking the notes in 3rds, name the triad from the key (I, II, IV or V — remember II is minor in a major key), then look at the lowest note to name the position. A IV chord with its 3rd in the bass reads as IVb.

teach.smartTip: The lowest note names the position, not the numeral. Find the root by stacking the notes in 3rds first, then check which member is in the bass: root = a, 3rd = b, 5th = c.
teach.didYouKnow: The little letters a, b and c are the ABRSM way of writing inversions. Elsewhere you may meet figured bass instead — IVb is the same chord a musician of Bach's day would have marked with a small 6 under the bass note.

objectives: A transposing instrument sounds at a different pitch from the note it reads — a B♭ clarinet, A clarinet and horn in F all SOUND LOWER than they are written
To make the instrument sound at concert pitch, write its part HIGHER than the concert note — up a major 2nd for a B♭ clarinet, a minor 3rd for an A clarinet, a perfect 5th for a horn in F
The written part takes the key signature of its transposed key, so the spelling comes from that key — not accidentals added against the concert key

concept.title: Transposing instruments
concept.body: Some instruments do not sound the note they read. A B♭ clarinet reads a written C but SOUNDS the B♭ a tone (major 2nd) below it; an A clarinet sounds a minor 3rd below; a horn in F sounds a perfect 5th below. Because the instrument sounds LOWER than written, you must write its part HIGHER than concert pitch by that same interval — so a concert-pitch line for a B♭ clarinet is written up a major 2nd. The written part sits in a new key, a major 2nd (or minor 3rd, or perfect 5th) higher than the concert key, and you notate it with THAT key's signature — the accidentals come from the key signature, not from marking each note. Concert C major written for a B♭ clarinet becomes D major.

teach.smartTip: Sounds lower → write higher. B♭ clarinet up a major 2nd, A clarinet up a minor 3rd, horn in F up a perfect 5th. Change the key signature to the transposed key and let it spell the notes.
teach.didYouKnow: Composers write for transposing instruments so a clarinettist can switch between the B♭ and A clarinet reading the SAME fingerings — the part is rewritten, but the hands do not have to relearn a thing.
